strengths: Introduces a unified framework (MotionLLaMA) covering the broadest range of motion-centric tasks reported (9 tasks spanning synthesis and comprehension, single- and dual-person), which is a meaningful step beyond prior Motion LLMs that typically support fewer tasks.

The proposed HoMi Tokenizer is a well-motivated design: separate body/hand encoders fused via MLP, plus a Frequency-Aware Motion Gating (bidirectional FFT + gating) module, achieving reconstruction quality on par with 6-codebook RVQ while using only a single codebook, which simplifies downstream LLM tokenization and mitigates RVQ's sampling complexity.

Construction of MotionHub, a large-scale aggregated multimodal, multitask motion dataset (single- and dual-person, text/audio-paired) sourced from many public datasets with careful re-annotation/standardization, is a useful community resource if released as claimed.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across many tasks (T2M, M2T, IT2M, M2D/D2M, S2G, motion completion/in-between) with comparisons to multiple baselines, plus ablations on tokenizer components, codebook size, and motion representation choices in the appendix.

Reports SOTA or near-SOTA results in several tasks (motion completion, dual-person T2M, most comprehension tasks) and comparable performance elsewhere, suggesting the unified approach does not catastrophically sacrifice per-task quality despite handling multiple tasks jointly.
weaknesses: Several quantitative results are mixed or below SOTA (e.g., M2D FID_k is not best on AIST++/FineDance, S2G FGD/L1Div are not top, single-person T2M R-precision/FID are behind MoMask/MotionDiffuse), yet the abstract/conclusion claims broad SOTA; the actual pattern is 'comparable to SOTA in most tasks, best in a few,' which is a more modest but still valid claim that could be stated more precisely.

The technical novelty of the HoMi Tokenizer (separate body/hand encoders, frequency-domain gating) is somewhat incremental relative to existing separate-part encoding works (e.g., HumanTomato, EMAGE) and frequency-based gating mechanisms used elsewhere; the ablation (Table 9) shows STH and FAMG each contribute but the overall reconstruction gain over vanilla VQ (Table 5) is more convincing than the incremental novelty argument.

No human perceptual studies or qualitative comparisons against strong single-task specialized SOTA on held-out unseen text prompts are provided beyond the automatic metrics; for generative tasks (T2M, M2D, S2G) automatic metrics like FID/diversity can be insufficiently correlated with perceived motion quality, and the visualizations (Fig. 5-6) are limited in number and lack quantitative failure-case analysis.

Limited analysis of computational cost/efficiency (model size, inference latency, training compute) despite claims of being a 'billion-level' LLM-based framework; no discussion of inference speed compared to diffusion or non-autoregressive baselines (e.g., MoMask), which is relevant given autoregressive token-by-token generation is typically slower.

The dataset construction pipeline relies heavily on ChatGPT-4o for caption generation/rewriting and manual annotation/filtering without reporting quality-control metrics (e.g., annotator agreement, caption quality validation), raising reproducibility and data-quality concerns for the claimed 'most exhaustive' dataset.

Ablation results in Table 9 for the tokenizer show the full model is not uniformly best on every axis (e.g., 'w/o FAMG' has better MPJPE-body than full model in some readings), and the paper doesn't discuss these nuances or provide statistical significance/variance across runs.

Some evaluation choices (e.g., training a new TMR feature extractor on MotionHub for dual-person tasks) make cross-paper comparability harder, since baselines are recomputed rather than using the exact protocols of the original papers, which could introduce discrepancies not fully addressed.

strengths: Presents a genuinely unified framework spanning nine motion-centric tasks (synthesis and comprehension, single- and dual-person), which is broader coverage than prior Motion LLMs (MotionGPT, LMM, M3GPT, UniMuMo, MotionAgent) as summarized in Table 1.

The HoMi Tokenizer is a solid technical contribution: separate hand/torso encoders plus a frequency-aware (FFT-based) gating mechanism allow a single codebook to match RVQ-level reconstruction accuracy while avoiding the sampling complexity of multi-codebook residual quantization; this is validated with a careful ablation (Table 9) and codebook-size analysis (Fig. 4, Table 12).

Introduces MotionHub, a large-scale, multi-modal (text/motion/audio), multi-task dataset built by aggregating and standardizing many existing motion sources with a clearly described curation pipeline (unified coordinate system, retargeting, manual annotation/filtering, and caption normalization), which should be a useful community resource if released as promised.

Extensive experimental coverage across nine tasks (T2M, M2T, M2D, D2M, S2G, motion completion/in-between, interaction T2M/M2T) with task-appropriate metrics, and the model achieves SOTA or near-SOTA results on several of them (interaction T2M, dual-person M2T, motion completion), plus a useful ablation on motion representation choices (Table 11) justifying the switch from HumanML3D-style features to global joint coordinates for multi-person compatibility.

Reasonable reproducibility support: architecture, training hyperparameters (LoRA rank/alpha, codebook sizes, special tokens), and evaluation protocols are described in detail, and code/dataset are stated to be publicly released.
weaknesses: On the core single-person T2M benchmark (Table 3), MotionLLaMA is not SOTA and in fact trails MoMask and MotionDiffuse on FID and R-precision, and it is also not SOTA on M2D (Table 6) and S2G (Table 8); the abstract's claim of SOTA on "the widest range" of tasks somewhat overstates this, since it is only comparable rather than best on several important synthesis tasks.

The MotionHub captions for datasets lacking native descriptions are generated via ChatGPT-4o rewriting/decomposition of interaction labels; no human evaluation or quality audit of these automatically generated captions is reported, leaving open questions about caption reliability that could affect downstream T2M/M2T evaluation validity.

The paper does not include an explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion (e.g., computational cost of LoRA fine-tuning a billion-parameter LLM per task, failure cases, or biases inherited from aggregated motion-capture datasets), which would strengthen the contextualization of the claims.

Some ablation comparisons are only briefly mentioned (e.g., the RVQ+Residual-Transformer comparison referenced in Sec. 4.7/4.8 is not shown in a table, only described qualitatively), limiting the ability to fully verify the reconstruction-vs-generation-quality argument.

Clarity could be improved in a few places, e.g., the encoding equation (Eq. 1) and gating mechanism description are somewhat terse, and it is not always clear which numbers in Tables 5/9/12 correspond to the exact same trained model instance versus different configurations.
